blocks.text: Reach for a heap when a problem keeps asking for **the smallest or largest of what's left** — while values are still being added or removed. Sorting answers that question once. A heap answers it again and again, at O(log n) per change.

blocks.alt: A table comparing three ways to keep values. A plain array finds the smallest in O(n), adds in O(1) and removes the smallest in O(n). A sorted array finds and removes the smallest in O(1) but adds in O(n), because values must shift. A heap finds the smallest in O(1) and adds or removes in O(log n).
blocks.caption: A heap is never the fastest at any one thing, but it's never slow at any of them.

blocks.text: That last row is the whole reason heaps exist. When a problem mixes **adding** values with **taking out the smallest (or largest)**, the other two choices each have one operation that costs O(n) — and a loop that does it n times costs O(n²).

items: **“k largest”, “k smallest”, “top k”, “k closest”, “k most frequent”** — keep a heap of size k.
**“Repeatedly take the smallest (or largest)”** — join the two shortest ropes, smash the two heaviest stones, run the most urgent task. A greedy choice made again and again.
**“Merge k sorted …”** — a heap holds the front of each list and always hands you the smallest of them.
**A stream with a running answer** — the kth largest so far, the median so far. Each new value costs O(log n).
**Scheduling and shortest paths** — events ordered by time, tasks by priority, Dijkstra's next-closest node.

blocks.text: Pattern 1: top k with a heap of size k

To find the **k smallest** values, keep a **max-heap** of the k smallest seen so far. When it grows past k, pop its top — the **largest** of them, which now can't be among the k smallest. At the end the heap holds exactly the answer.
A max-heap for the *smallest*? Yes: the heap's top should be the value you'll throw out next — the **worst** of the ones you're keeping.

blocks.alt: Finding the 3 smallest of 5, 1, 9, 3, 7, 2 with a max-heap that never keeps more than 3 values. After 5, 1 and 9 the heap holds 9, 1, 5 with 9 on top. Adding 3 makes 4 values, so the largest, 9, is dropped. Adding 7 makes 4 again and 7 itself is dropped. Adding 2 drops 5. The heap ends with 3, 2, 1: the three smallest.
blocks.caption: The heap never holds more than k + 1 values, so each step costs O(log k).

blocks.text: **Time O(n log k), space O(k).** Sorting would cost O(n log n) and need every value in memory at once; this works on a stream and only ever holds k + 1 values. For the **k largest**, flip it: a **min**-heap whose top is the smallest of the kept values.
In this course: **Kth Largest Element in a Stream**, **Kth Largest Element in an Array**, **K Closest Points to Origin** and **Top K Frequent Elements**.
Pattern 2: always take the smallest (or largest)
Some problems are a loop of the same greedy move: take the one or two most extreme values, combine them, put the result back. A heap makes each round O(log n) instead of a fresh sort.

blocks.alt: Joining ropes of length 4, 3, 2 and 6, always joining the two shortest. Join 2 and 3 for a cost of 5; the ropes are now 4, 5, 6. Join 4 and 5 for 9; the ropes are now 6, 9. Join 6 and 9 for 15. The total cost is 5 plus 9 plus 15, which is 29.

To merge k sorted lists, you only ever need to compare their **fronts**. Keep the k fronts in a min-heap: pop the smallest into the output, then push the next value from the same list. Each output value costs O(log k).

blocks.alt: Three sorted lists, 1 4 7, 2 5 8 and 3 6 9. Their fronts, 1, 2 and 3, sit in a min-heap. The heap hands out 1, the smallest front; then 4, the next value of the first list, joins the heap.

blocks.text: In this course: **Sort a K-Sorted Array**, **Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix** and **Merge K Sorted Lists**.
Pattern 4: two heaps for a running middle

Split the values into a **lower half** kept in a max-heap and an **upper half** kept in a min-heap. The two tops are the two middle values, so the median is always O(1) away, and each new value costs O(log n).

blocks.alt: The values 5, 2, 8, 1, 9 and 3 split into two halves. The lower half, 1, 2 and 3, sits in a max-heap with 3 on top. The upper half, 5, 8 and 9, sits in a min-heap with 5 on top. The median is the average of the two tops, 3 and 5, which is 4.

blocks.text: In this course: **Find Median from Data Stream**.
When a heap is the wrong tool

items: **You need everything in order, once.** Just sort: O(n log n), simpler, and often faster in practice.
**You only need the smallest value once.** One pass with a variable is O(n) and O(1) space.

**You need to find or delete arbitrary values.** A heap only knows where its top is; searching it is O(n). Use a **hash map**, or a balanced tree (`TreeMap` in Java, `std::set` in C++) when you also need order.
**You need both the smallest and the largest, repeatedly.** One heap gives only one end cheaply. Use two heaps, or a balanced tree.
A heap shines when **adding** values is mixed with **taking out the smallest or largest**.
**Top k**: a heap of size k whose top is the next to throw out — O(n log k).
**Greedy rounds**, **k-way merges** and **running medians** are the other three heap patterns.
If you only need sorted order once, sort. If you need lookups by value, use a hash map.
